strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored evaluation gap: geometric perception as a foundational capability for MLLMs, distinct from high-level semantic and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
Introduces a large-scale synthetic benchmark (80K figures, 285K multiple-choice questions) covering six geometric aspects with easy/hard splits, plus human validation showing 99.3% average accuracy.
Provides a broad zero-shot evaluation of 20 closed- and open-source MLLMs, with useful ablations on visual encoders and shape-count complexity.

Shows a plausible downstream-transfer experiment by training LLaVA-GeP on the synthetic data and evaluating on general and math/chart benchmarks, suggesting geometric perception may benefit other tasks.
The data engine and benchmark design are clearly motivated and, if released, could support future diagnostic studies of spatial and geometric failures in MLLMs.
weaknesses: The benchmark is entirely synthetic and rendered with Matplotlib, using simple abstract shapes and limited noise; it does not establish that performance transfers to real-world geometric perception, hand-drawn diagrams, occlusions, perspective, or domain-specific images such as medical or scientific figures.

Several models perform below random guessing on the 'size' aspect, which is a serious validity red flag. This may indicate ambiguous question/option generation, non-uniform answer distributions, parsing errors, prompt artifacts, or a mismatch between the task and visual encoder capabilities. The paper does not analyze this anomaly, so the claim that it reveals a fundamental geometric deficiency is not fully supported.

Downstream gains from LLaVA-GeP are modest (2.2% average) and lack statistical significance testing, multiple seeds, or confidence intervals, making it unclear whether the improvements are robust rather than noise.

There are internal inconsistencies and missing details: human evaluation is described as 200 questions per aspect in one place and 1,000 in the appendix; LLaVA-GeP training is described as full finetuning in one place and LoRA in another; generation reproduce details such as seeds, distractor sampling, overlap threshold, and relationship constraints are incomplete.

The synthetic benchmark has limited novelty relative to prior procedural/CLEVR-style datasets and spatial-reasoning benchmarks; the paper does not sufficiently compare against existing geometric or abstract-visual benchmarks beyond mathematical geometry datasets.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code and data are promised, but the generation engine, parsing pipeline, exact prompts, and training scripts are not fully specified in the manuscript. It is also unclear whether evaluation data are contamination-free relative to LLaVA-GeP training.

The limitations section is superficial and omits the most important issues: synthetic-to-real gap, below-random subset behavior, absence of statistical significance in downstream gains, and lack of IRB/consent details for human evaluation.

Presentation quality has multiple issues: reference formatting is inconsistent, typos and capitalization errors appear throughout, and key algorithm/data-generation details are too vague for readers to fully assess or reproduce the benchmark.

strengths: Targets a genuine and underexplored capability: foundational geometric perception (spatial awareness, shape recognition, relationship understanding) as distinct from the high-level semantic/reasoning focus of existing MLLM benchmarks (GQA, MMMU, MathVista, GeoQA, etc.).

Provides a large-scale, structured generation pipeline (Algorithm 1, Section 3.1-3.3) that generates figures, structured descriptions, and multiple-choice questions in a reproducible, self-consistent way, and includes human validation (99.3% average accuracy, Section 3.4) confirming the tasks are well-defined and solvable for humans.

Comprehensive zero-shot evaluation of 20 MLLMs across six question aspects and easy/hard splits (Table 1), plus useful ablations on visual encoders (Table 2), number of shapes (Figure 5), and noise (Appendix E.2).

Includes a downstream transfer experiment (Section 4.5) with a legitimate control (a LLaVA-1.5-7B trained from scratch under the same procedure), which is a reasonable attempt to test the 'foundational' hypothesis.
weaknesses: The strongest headline results are not adequately diagnosed for validity. GPT-4o scoring 17.5% and Claude 17.9% on 'size', and many models falling below the 25% random-guess floor, is a red flag that typically indicates ambiguous/ill-posed items, distractor design problems (numeric-interval answers), or answer-parsing failures rather than pure capability deficits. The paper attributes this to visual-encoder transformation invariance (Section 4.2) without any verification (e.g., item-level error analysis, paraphrase robustness, or log-likelihood scoring). If models are far below chance, the benchmark may not be measuring what the authors claim.

Limited originality. Synthetic geometry corpora and generation engines already exist (GeoQA, Geometry3K, UniGeo, GeoVerse, GeoMM, MAVIS-Instruct), and the proposed 'perception vs reasoning' distinction is blurry: the 'size' questions (e.g., 'what is the area of the rectangle?') and 'relationship' questions involve numeric estimation and relational inference that overlap substantially with existing geometry-reasoning benchmarks.

The central claim that geometric perception is a 'foundational' ability enabling higher-level tasks is weakly supported. LLaVA-GeP improves by only ~2.2% on average, and the training mixes 300K new pretraining captions and 240K new instruction samples into the original LLaVA data, so gains cannot be cleanly attributed to geometric perception as opposed to additional task-agnostic instruction/pretraining data.

Ecological validity is asserted rather than demonstrated. Matplotlib-rendered synthetic figures with artificial noise may not reflect real-world geometric perception, and the claimed relevance to medical imaging and fossil classification (Section 1) is aspirational and untested.

Presentation/consistency issues: human-evaluation sample sizes conflict between Section 3.4 ('200 questions per aspect') and Appendix B.3 ('1,000 questions ... per aspect'); the scaling discussion labels 5.0-9.5% gains as 'limited' without a principled criterion; and the figure-quality/legend details in Figures 3-7 are difficult to interpret as presented.

strengths: Identifies an important and underexplored capability: geometric perception for multimodal LLMs, complementing existing benchmarks that emphasize high-level semantics or mathematical reasoning.

Constructs a large-scale synthetic benchmark with 80K images and 285K multiple-choice questions spanning six diagnostic aspects (existence, counting, size, location, reference, relationship) and easy/hard splits.
Provides an extensive empirical study of 20 closed- and open-source MLLMs, plus human evaluation (99.3% average accuracy) and analyses of scaling, visual encoders, and injected visual noise.

The data synthesis engine and visual noise injection offer a controllable way to stress-test low-level visual/spatial perception, and the human baseline supports that the tasks are generally solvable.
The downstream LLaVA-GeP experiment provides suggestive evidence that geometric-perception-style training data may improve several general, math, and chart benchmarks.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity is not sufficiently established: synthetic line renderings, overlaps, intersections, and template distractors can produce ambiguous or unintended shapes, especially for counting/existence/reference questions. The relationship example in Figure 1 also appears to have an option/answer mismatch (B is 'parallel' but the answer says 'B. circumscribed'), raising concerns about label consistency unless it is only a typo.

Novelty is limited relative to prior synthetic visual-reasoning datasets such as CLEVR and related spatial-reasoning benchmarks, which are not discussed. GePBench largely resembles established synthetic geometric/spatial diagnostics, differing mainly in its application to modern MLLMs and added geometric relationship types.

Reproducibility is weak: the generation algorithm leaves out critical details such as distractor construction, filtering thresholds, question templates, split assignment, seeds, and relationship enforcement. Code and datasets are only promised to be released, not available; training and LLM-judge details are also incomplete.

Evaluation rigor is limited: only a single zero-shot run is reported, with no confidence intervals or significance tests; resizing all images to 640x640 may disadvantage models with native variable-resolution processing; answer parsing uses a heuristic validated on only 100 responses per model.

The downstream claim is confounded: LLaVA-GeP is trained with additional geometry data mixed into LLaVA's original training data, but there is no control for extra data volume or non-geometric additional data. The model is not evaluated on a held-out GePBench test set, and no contamination checks are reported.

Human evaluation and ethics reporting are incomplete: consent/IRB procedures are not documented, inter-annotator agreement is absent, and the number/sampling of human-annotated questions is ambiguously reported. The limitations section omits synthetic-to-real gaps, ambiguity/label noise, contamination, and reproducibility constraints.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports: the benchmark failures may partly reflect synthetic distribution shift rather than a fundamental lack of geometric perception, and the downstream gains do not causally establish that geometric perception plays a 'critical role' in higher-level multimodal tasks.
